subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 68-year-old man dies 5 days after an acute myocardial infarction. At autopsy, a section of the left ventricular free wall shows a well-demarcated region of pale, firm tissue. Microscopy shows that the architecture of the myocardium is preserved, with surviving cell outlines, but the nuclei are no longer visible and the cytoplasm stains intensely pink with eosin.
question: Which of the following best describes this type of necrosis?

options.text: Coagulative necrosis, in which denatured enzymes block proteolysis
Liquefactive necrosis from lysosomal enzymes of neutrophils
Caseous necrosis with granulomatous walling off of debris
Fat necrosis with saponification of triglycerides
Fibrinoid necrosis with immune complex deposition in vessel walls

explanation_correct: Coagulative necrosis occurs with ischemia and infarction in most tissues other than the brain. Ischemic injury denatures structural proteins and enzymes, so proteolysis is blocked and the underlying cellular architecture remains visible even though the nuclei disappear. The increased cytoplasmic binding of eosin stain produces the classic red or pink appearance with prominent eosinophilia, exactly as seen in this infarct.

explanation_incorrect.A: Liquefactive necrosis results from neutrophils releasing lysosomal enzymes that digest tissue, producing early cellular debris and macrophages and later cystic spaces; it occurs in bacterial abscesses and CNS infarcts, not in a typical myocardial infarct.
explanation_incorrect.B: Caseous necrosis arises when macrophages wall off an organism such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Histoplasma capsulatum, yielding fragmentation and debris surrounded by a granuloma with a cheeselike gross appearance.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fat necrosis involves the outlines of dead fat cells without peripheral nuclei and saponification when liberated fatty acids bind calcium; the heart is not a site of fat necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is confined to blood vessel walls, where an eosinophilic layer of proteinaceous material accumulates after immune complex deposition or plasma protein leakage.

educationalObjective: Coagulative necrosis follows ischemia in all tissues except the brain; denatured enzymes block proteolysis, so cell outlines persist while nuclei vanish and the cytoplasm becomes brightly eosinophilic.

subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 64-year-old woman presents with the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and aphasia. Imaging shows an acute infarct in the left middle cerebral artery territory. She does not survive the hospitalization, and at autopsy the infarcted area is soft and partially cystic with loss of normal tissue architecture and numerous macrophages containing debris.
question: Which of the following explains why this infarct differs from most ischemic infarcts?

options.text: Ischemic injury denatured enzymes, preserving cellular outlines
Neutrophil lysosomal enzymes digested the tissue, causing cavitation
Macrophages walled off the infarct, producing granular debris
Fatty acids from damaged cells bound calcium in the infarct
Immune complexes deposited within the walls of cerebral arterioles

explanation_correct: The brain is the classic exception to coagulative necrosis: ischemic infarction in the central nervous system produces liquefactive necrosis instead. Neutrophils release lysosomal enzymes that digest the dead tissue, so early on there is cellular debris with macrophages and later there are cystic spaces and cavitation, which is why the infarcted area became soft and cystic. Coagulative necrosis, in which denaturation of enzymes blocks proteolysis, occurs in ischemic injury of most other solid organs such as the heart and kidney.

explanation_incorrect.B: Denaturation of enzymes with preserved cell outlines is precisely the mechanism of coagulative necrosis, which spares the brain; it is the pattern this patient does not have.
explanation_incorrect.C: Granular debris walled off by macrophages forming a granuloma describes caseous necrosis, which follows infection with tuberculosis or certain fungi rather than infarction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Binding of calcium by liberated fatty acids is saponification in fat necrosis, which occurs in peripancreatic fat or traumatized breast tissue, not in cerebral infarction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Immune complex deposition in vessel walls causes fibrinoid necrosis of small arteries in vasculitis; it does not liquefy brain parenchyma.

educationalObjective: The brain and CNS are the exception: ischemic infarction there causes liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis, with enzymatic digestion, debris, and eventual cystic cavitation.

subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 45-year-old man with a history of untreated HIV infection and a low CD4 count presents with fever, weight loss, and a cavitary lesion in the upper lobe of the right lung. A biopsy reveals fragmented cells and amorphous debris surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes and macrophages, with multinucleated giant cells. On cut section the lesion has a soft, cheesy, crumbly appearance.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: Coagulative necrosis with preserved alveolar architecture
Liquefactive necrosis forming a cyst with a thin fibrous wall
Caseous necrosis within a granulomatous response
Dystrophic calcification of a resolved granuloma
Fat necrosis with chalky-white saponified fat

explanation_correct: Caseous necrosis is classically produced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as well as by systemic fungi such as Histoplasma capsulatum and by Nocardia. Macrophages wall off the organism, generating granular debris that appears surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, and giant cells in a granuloma, and grossly as a cheeselike material. The combination of caseation and granulomatous rim in an immunocompromised patient with an upper lobe cavity is the classic picture of tuberculosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Coagulative necrosis results from ischemia and preserves cell outlines while nuclei disappear; it does not produce a granulomatous rim with giant cells or a cheesy gross appearance.
explanation_incorrect.B: Liquefactive necrosis from neutrophilic lysosomal enzymes yields cellular debris, macrophages, and cystic spaces, typically in bacterial abscesses and CNS infarcts, not the walled-off granular debris of caseation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Calcification is mineralization of necrotic tissue and follows caseation over time; it appears as deeply basophilic deposits rather than the soft, cheesy, crumbly material described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fat necrosis from lipase activity involves saponification of adipocytes and appears chalky white, usually in peripancreatic fat in acute pancreatitis or after breast trauma.

educationalObjective: Caseous necrosis occurs with tuberculosis and systemic fungi such as Histoplasma capsulatum; macrophages wall off the organism, forming a granuloma with granular debris and a cheeselike gross appearance.

subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 46-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and markedly elevated serum lipase. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography shows ill-defined fluid collections with chalky-white areas surrounding the pancreas. Biopsy of the peripancreatic tissue shows shadowy outlines of dead adipocytes lacking peripheral nuclei, with basophilic material deposited in the fat.
question: Which of the following is responsible for the chalky-white and basophilic material in this tissue?

options.text: Binding of liberated fatty acids to calcium, producing saponification
IgG and fibrin deposition within arteriolar walls from immune complexes
Enzymatic denaturation with preserved architectural outlines
Lysosomal enzymes of neutrophils digesting the fat into a cavity
Deposition of protein in a beta-pleated sheet with Congo red uptake

explanation_correct: In fat necrosis, damaged pancreatic cells release lipase, which breaks down triglycerides; the liberated fatty acids then bind calcium, producing saponification with a chalky-white gross appearance. Histologically the dead fat cells retain outlines but lose their peripheral nuclei, and the saponified fat combined with calcium appears dark blue on the H&E stain. The same nonenzymatic mechanism can follow trauma to breast tissue.

explanation_incorrect.A: Immune complex and fibrin deposition in vessel walls is fibrinoid necrosis, seen in immune vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, and it does not produce chalky fat.
explanation_incorrect.C: Denaturation of enzymes with preserved outlines is coagulative necrosis, which describes cells rather than the saponified adipocytes with basophilic deposits seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Neutrophilic digestion producing a cavity is liquefactive necrosis; saponification requires lipase-mediated hydrolysis of triglycerides, not leukocyte enzymes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Beta-pleated sheet protein that binds Congo red is amyloid, which stains amorphous pink on H&E and shows apple-green birefringence, not the chalky basophilic fat described.

educationalObjective: Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis results from lipase-mediated triglyceride breakdown and saponification, with fatty acids binding calcium to give a chalky-white, dark blue on H&E appearance.

subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 54-year-old woman presents with fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, and painful erythematous nodules on the lower legs. She has mononeuritis multiplex with foot drop, and laboratory testing shows an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and hepatitis B surface antigen positivity. Biopsy of the nodules reveals an affected medium-sized vessel with an eosinophilic, proteinaceous layer within its wall.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the vessel lesion?

options.text: Fibrinoid necrosis from immune complex deposition, as in polyarteritis nodosa
Coagulative necrosis of the vessel wall caused by ischemia
Caseous necrosis within a vessel in a granulomatous vasculitis
Liquefactive necrosis with cavitation of the vessel lumen
Fat necrosis with saponification in the vessel wall

explanation_correct: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in immune vascular reactions such as polyarteritis nodosa, where immune complex deposition, a type III hypersensitivity reaction, plus plasma protein and fibrin leakage from the damaged vessel create an eosinophilic layer of proteinaceous material in the wall. Hepatitis B surface antigen is the classic association with polyarteritis nodosa, which typically produces systemic symptoms, skin nodules, and mononeuritis multiplex; the same appearance arises from nonimmune vascular injury in a hypertensive emergency or preeclampsia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Coagulative necrosis results from ischemia, with enzymatic denaturation and preserved cell outlines; this lesion instead deposits immune complexes and leaked plasma proteins within a vessel wall.
explanation_incorrect.B: Caseous necrosis is a granulomatous pattern seen with tuberculosis and systemic fungi, not the fibrinoid change of medium vessel vasculitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Liquefactive necrosis with cavitation follows neutrophilic enzymatic digestion in abscesses and CNS infarcts; it is not the description of an eosinophilic vessel wall layer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fat necrosis from lipase action affects adipose tissue, as in acute pancreatitis, and has no role in immune complex deposition in arterioles.

educationalObjective: Fibrinoid necrosis reflects immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) or nonimmune plasma protein leakage in vessel walls, and is seen with polyarteritis nodosa, hypertensive emergency, and preeclampsia.

subject: Pathology
subtopic: Necrosis types: coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid
vignette: A 70-year-old man with advanced peripheral arterial disease develops a black, dry, shriveled lesion involving the toes and distal foot. He has no fever and no purulent drainage. Two weeks later, after a minor abrasion, the same area becomes swollen, foul-smelling, and wet, and cultures grow multiple organisms including anaerobes.
question: Which of the following best describes the gangrenous change in this patient's foot?

options.text: Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis, and wet gangrene superimposes liquefactive necrosis
Dry gangrene is liquefactive necrosis, and wet gangrene superimposes caseous necrosis
Both forms represent caseous necrosis within a granuloma
Both forms represent fibrinoid necrosis of the digital arteries
Dry gangrene is fat necrosis, and wet gangrene is metastatic calcification

explanation_correct: Gangrenous necrosis affects the distal extremities and gastrointestinal tract after chronic ischemia. Dry gangrene results from ischemia alone and has the underlying appearance of coagulative necrosis, matching the black, dry, shriveled, shrunken tissue. Wet gangrene occurs when the necrotic tissue becomes superinfected, superimposing liquefactive necrosis on the coagulative necrosis, which explains the abrupt development of swelling, foul odor, and purulent exudate.

explanation_incorrect.A: The mapping is reversed: ischemic dry gangrene shows coagulative necrosis, and it is superinfection that adds liquefactive rather than caseous necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Caseous necrosis requires a granulomatous response to organisms such as tuberculosis or Histoplasma and does not describe chronic ischemic injury to a limb.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fibrinoid necrosis is a lesion of individual vessel walls in immune or hypertensive injury, not the regional tissue destruction of gangrene of a digit.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fat necrosis is lipase-mediated saponification of adipose tissue, and metastatic calcification is calcium deposition in normal tissues from hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia; neither defines gangrene.

educationalObjective: Dry gangrene is ischemic and therefore coagulative, whereas wet gangrene reflects superinfection, which superimposes liquefactive necrosis on the coagulative pattern.
